speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It supports economic policies that promote domestic and global financial stability and foster the economic well-being of countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The IMF depends on its members to provide the necessary financial resources to carry out its mission.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This refers to each member's capital subscription in the IMF that is broadly based on the member's relative position in the global economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: As a small, highly open economy, and a responsible member of the international community, it is in Singapore's interest to support the IMF's multilateral efforts to promote financial stability and strengthen the resilience of the global financial and monetary system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Under the Bretton Woods Agreements Act (BWAA), MAS is empowered to enter into agreements on behalf of the Government of Singapore to provide loans, grants or other financial assistance in support of IMF arrangements or programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is subject to safeguards, set out in section 6A of BWAA, that ensure the proper exercise of MAS' powers in relation to this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: First, the Bill proposes amendments to clarify that the safeguards which relate to grants in sections 6A(2) and (3) of BWAA are intended to apply to grants provided to help member countries under IMF arrangements or programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: They are not intended to apply to grants provided to fund the IMF's offices in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Second, the Bill proposes amendments to the early repayment requirement in section 6A(4) of BWAA to take into account: one, the IMF's use of standard-form agreements, and that, two, some of its arrangements or programmes cannot be suspended or prematurely terminated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: I wish to emphasise that the proposed amendments remain consistent with, and do not detract from, the intent of the existing safeguards in section 6A, which is to ensure the proper exercise of MAS' powers in relation to the provision of loans, grants or other financial assistance to the IMF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The first set of amendments relates to the safeguards in section 6A(2) and (3) of BWAA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These safeguards apply when MAS enters into an agreement to provide a grant to the IMF to support IMF arrangements or programmes with member countries in need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Under BWAA, MAS has provided various grants to the IMF for this purpose.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: For example, MAS provided three grants in 2021, as part of multilateral efforts to enhance the capacity of the IMF to assist member countries, including in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Separately, MAS, on behalf of the Government of Singapore, funds two IMF offices which we host in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The two offices are: First, the IMF-Singapore Regional Training Institute (IMF-STI).

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This is the IMF's regional training centre for the Asia and Pacific Region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Its mission is to enhance the economic and policymaking capacity of countries in the region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS co-funds the IMF-STI with IMF, our Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as the Government of Japan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Second, the IMF Resident Representative Office in Singapore (IMF RRO).

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This serves as a liaison office between IMF and Singapore and assists with the IMF's macroeconomic surveillance work in the region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS co-funds the IMF RRO with the IMF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Grants provided to finance the IMF's offices in Singapore are different from grants provided to support IMF arrangements or programmes which assist member countries in need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: When Singapore contributes grants to the IMF to support its arrangements or programmes to assist member countries in need, we depend on the IMF management and Executive Board to ensure proper governance in the administration of the grants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: It would, therefore, be prudent to subject such grants to additional safeguards in section 6A of BWAA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These safeguards include ensuring that: One, any grant provided is pursuant to a specific request from the IMF; Two, any grant is provided only as part of a multilateral effort by IMF members; Three, there is transparency in the form of a Gazette notice covering the key information of the assistance; and Four, Parliament approves grants by specific resolution.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In contrast, grants to finance the IMF's offices in Singapore support IMF's operations and functions in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The scope of this financing is clearly set out in memoranda of understanding entered into between the Government of Singapore and IMF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: MAS exercises oversight on the use of these funds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In addition, MAS' financing of the IMF offices in Singapore is currently subsumed under MAS' overall annual budget and approved on a consolidated basis by the President, in accordance with the budget approval process under the MAS Act of 1970.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: BWAA will, therefore, be amended to clarify that agreements to provide grants to finance the operations and functions of the IMF's offices in Singapore are not subject to the safeguards in sections 6A(2) and (3).

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: To be clear, agreements to provide grants to support IMF arrangements or programmes to assist member countries that are in need will remain subject to the safeguards in sections 6A(2) and (3), including the requirement for Parliamentary approval.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The second set of amendments relates to section 6A(4) of BWAA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: These apply when MAS enters into an agreement to provide a loan or other financial assistance, excluding grants, to support an IMF arrangement or programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Section 6A(4) requires that such agreements include provisions that allow MAS to require early repayment in the event of suspension or premature termination of the IMF arrangement or programme for which the assistance was provided.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This early repayment requirement is in addition to existing provisions in MAS' loan agreements with IMF, which oblige IMF to immediately repay the loan in the event of a balance of payments need in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The intent of the early repayment requirement was to provide additional assurance that MAS would be able to recover its monies from IMF, even if we have no balance of payments need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: In practice, however, IMF is unable to accommodate requests from MAS to include this early repayment requirement in IMF arrangements or programmes which are multilateral in nature and use the IMF's standard-form agreements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: IMF is required to ensure uniformity and equity of treatment for all contributing members and cannot provide for early repayment to any one contributing member, short of a contributing member having a balance of payments need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: IMF has also indicated that certain IMF arrangements or programmes cannot be suspended or prematurely terminated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: There are also further safeguards in relation to loans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: First, when Singapore provides a loan in support of the IMF arrangements or programmes, Singapore lends to the IMF and not directly to a member country in need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: Amidst the uncertain global economic environment and rising geopolitical tensions, IMF is a key pillar of the multilateral system that fosters cooperation and promotes shared interests in the international financial system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Prime Minister)
text: The proposed amendments will enable Singapore to contribute to the work and mission of IMF as a responsible member of the international community, in a prudent manner that fulfils the intent of BWAA and ensures the proper exercise of MAS' powers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support the Bill, but I have a few points of clarification.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bretton Woods Agreement, signed in 1944, resulted in the creation of the IMF and the World Bank.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While these institutions have played important roles in global economic stability and development, I feel that they face challenges in addressing the complex issue of climate change.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Through our Government's fulfilment of our commitment to IMF, can Singapore influence IMF to prioritise climate change as a central component of its operations?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This may include integrating climate considerations into their policies, lending practices and technical assistance programmes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As mentioned by Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam on 8 June 2023, MAS aims to bring together philanthropies, multilateral development banks, development finance institutions and donor partners to channel blended finance at scale into transition and green infrastructure projects into the region.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope MAS can invite IMF to come on board as IMF also has the means to provide adequate financial support to emerging countries for climate mitigation and adaptation efforts.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: IMF can play a role in facilitating this coordination by fostering dialogue and collaboration between developed and developing countries, as well as providing technical assistance in developing climate‐related policies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, IMF can broker more carbon credit cooperation between the developing countries and Singapore, so that there is a good range of carbon credits for our large carbon emitters to choose from in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although not directly related to this Bill, but since the Singapore Government funds the operations of IMF's offices in Singapore, can Singapore be given priority to support IMF's capacity‐building efforts in providing training, knowledge sharing and technical assistance on climate‐related topics to member countries?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can MAS and IMF jointly provide some form of "aircover" or support to the financial institutions in Singapore so that they will be incentivised to provide transition finance to the brown industries in the region?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will certainly boost Singapore's capacity as well as status as a green economy hub.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is affirmed by a recent article published by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research, which states that many Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) countries face the challenge of reducing greenhouse emissions while at the same time expanding energy supply to meet the needs of their rapidly developing economies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Where is Singapore in the repayment pecking order?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I just want to make sure that Singapore's interest is not being compromised and agreements are entered into on a pari passu basis.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that there is no stipulated repayment date.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, does this mean that Singapore cannot take back the grant in the event Singapore has an emergency?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If this is the case, why would Singapore want to provide such a grant?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate that by supporting IMF, Singapore can also contribute to poverty reduction, improved infrastructure and increased access to clean energy in developing countries.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This, in turn, can foster economic growth and stability, benefiting the global economy which Singapore is part of.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, while I support the Bill, I have some comments, both on the specific contents of the Bill being considered, as well as one – on the use of SDRs – that is fully within the spirit of the Bill but is not directly taken up by it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clause 3(a) of the Bill was included to preclude the use of grants for the funding of IMF offices hosted in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This sort of ringfencing strikes me as eminently sensible, since we do not want BWAA to inadvertently become a funnel for grants to the Fund via MAS without Parliamentary approval.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, it is curious to me why the amendment does not include or require associated changes to the International Development Association (IDA) Act, since IDA similarly provides grants, funded from subscriptions, even as the World Bank maintains offices here, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If such language was already included in the most recent amendment to the IDA Act, tabled in October of last year, I was unable to find it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps the Minister of State may clarify as to why this allied amendment is unnecessary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, a cursory examination of the website for IMF-STI reveals just 16 staff members, compared to the World Bank's Singapore Infrastructure and Urban Hub, which is the largest operational office co-locating staff from the Bank, approximating some 200 or so professionals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will now move on to my main constructive suggestion, offered in the spirit of the Bill, about how we can better use SDRs for the purposes of foreign assistance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In August 2021, IMF made a general SDR allocation to all member countries of IMF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It was meant to help countries get through the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To ensure the integrity of the process and to encourage donations, the Fund established two trusts: the PRGT and the Resilience and Sustainability Trust (RST), where countries with excess SDRs could make transfers into.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While not meant to be a substitute for actual foreign aid, reallocating SDRs to countries that have struggled with accessing financing after the COVID-19 crisis is very much meant to be complementary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Advanced economies already had an easier time tapping on financial resources as they rolled out their support packages, since many were able to easily issue debt at low cost in private markets.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, by dint of the SDR quota formula, developed countries received two-thirds the share of the total SDR injection, despite having a fifth of the population.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The crunch was most acute for the least developed countries, since their SDR allocation only came up to 2.4% of the total.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The proposed amendments to the language of the Bill, specifically clause 2, which replaces how the MAS is not just constrained to "buy or sell" SDRs alone, but also "otherwise deal with" them, explicitly opens the door for SDRs to also be reallocated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this Government has already taken some steps in the direction of offering grants, as well as doing so specifically with SDRs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In January this year, the Government provided an additional subscription of up to $70 million to the World Bank's IDA, which offers grants to the world’s poorest countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And two years ago, the Government proposed grants to three separate funds led by IMF, using SDRs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For the latter grants, Minister Ong Ye Kung had moved that the grants of $17.6 million be made to the Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust, $2 million to the COVID-19 Crisis Capacity Development Initiative, and $0.97 million to a special debt relief programme for Somalia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Together, these come up to a little less than $21 million dollars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we think we should be prudent with re-allocations, it is worth pointing out that the amounts we have transferred so far are only a fifth of the amounts we have already pledged – we offered a billion – and we only supported one of the two recommended trust funds, which is the RST.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, transferring our SDR allocations are not costless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the allocations we received in 2021 were, indeed, cost-free, they did not require contributions from our fiscal budget, nor add to our debt burden – something that Minister of State Alvin Tan had mentioned – and they remain so only if they remain held as part of our foreign exchange reserves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Should we use our SDRs by exchanging it for hard currencies and giving the resulting amount away as a grant, or alternatively by directly transferring these SDRs to other needy nations, we will, indeed, incur net charges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, transferring an amount less than 100 times our quota allocation does not strike me as, in the words of Minister Ong Ye Kung at that time, "commensurate with our size".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After all, while it is true that our quota and voting rights at the Fund are determined by a formula, how much we offer of this as a contribution is limited only by our desire.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If, indeed, we are, again in Minister Ong Ye Kung's words, "always struggling for relevance", I can think of more difficult ways than to demonstrate our presence, despite our size, via our generosity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And this brings me back to a theme that I have repeatedly shared with this House: that the good faith delivery of foreign aid helps not just the countries that we support, but can also rebound back to us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And when these countries become richer, they are more able to afford the sorts of higher value-added goods and services economies, such as our own, produce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the moral impetus to support other economies is also strong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such goodwill can be very valuable when we hope for support from other nations sometime in the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a small country, this sort of soft power can only be disproportionately obtained by building up a stock today, by being generous when others are needy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The two organisations continue to play a key role in facilitating cooperation among more than 180 member countries to promote financial stability and monetary cooperation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many would not know that Singapore officially joined the World Bank on 3 August 1966, shortly after Independence from Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We contribute not only because we should give back to the international community, but also because a prosperous and growing global economic environment is important to our open, trade-dependent economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When we debated the addition of section 6A back in 2016, I noted the strong safeguards applicable for Singapore to provide loans, grants and other forms of financial assistance to IMF for its arrangements and programmes, including the need for Parliament's approval in the case of grants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Since the introduction of section 6A, I would like to ask the Minister of State how many times has MAS agreed to provide financial assistance under that section.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what is the total value of such financial assistance, including loans and grants?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the 2016 debate, various Members, including myself, noted that not many Singaporeans would learn of the amounts of assistance we are providing to other countries by looking up the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Turning to the present amendment Bill, what is the reason for removing the safeguards in relation to agreements to finance the operations and functions of IMF offices in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While I can see the rationale for disapplying subsection (2)(b), which was "incorporated to preclude Singapore from making grants to the IMF purely on our own  ", why is the funding of IMF offices in Singapore excused from Parliamentary oversight of the maximum amount of grants that can be given by MAS?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I understand that there are two such IMF offices in Singapore: the IMF-STI and IMF RRO.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I actually went for a few courses in IMF-STI when I was in MAS – valuable training courses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what is the function of each office going forward and how do they benefit Singapore?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As any grant to IMF would be an expense that reduces the amount we accumulate in Singapore's Official Foreign Reserves (OFR), who would exercise oversight over the MAS' discretion if it is not Parliament?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also note that the constitutional check by the Elected President would not apply where Past Reserves are not being touched.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whereas the Act currently provides that any loan agreement must provide MAS with the right to require early repayment upon the suspension or premature termination of the IMF arrangement or programme, such a rule would not apply to a standard form agreement provided by IMF, or if the IMF arrangement or programme cannot be suspended or prematurely terminated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In relation to the first class of exempted agreements, I am concerned that this would cover the majority of instances where IMF requests Singapore to provide assistance in support of an IMF arrangement or programme for the benefit of one or more countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps the Minister of State or Minister can share, based on the previous requests Singapore has received from IMF, what percentage involved "standard form agreements" which cannot be unilaterally amended by MAS?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In relation to the second class of exempted agreements, I am curious what would be an example of an IMF arrangement or programme which cannot be suspended or prematurely terminated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even as we do that, we must stay true to our enduring quality of prudence in public spending.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Every expense is an amount that could otherwise be accumulated into our official Reserves, which we know are there to tide us through major crises like the recent COVID-19 pandemic and for many crises in the future.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will first address Mr Don Wee's questions relating to the IMF's role in dealing with climate change.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In line with the IMF's mandate to promote global macroeconomic and financial stability, and recognising that climate change can pose a significant risk to members' economic well-being, IMF has stepped up efforts to incorporate climate considerations and goals across its surveillance, lending and capacity development activities.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On surveillance, IMF provides guidance to members on appropriate macroeconomic and fiscal policies that facilitate climate mitigation, adaptation and the transition to a low-carbon economy.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: IMF incorporates climate risk analysis into its Financial Sector Assessment Programmes to assess the impact of climate change on the stability of members' financial sectors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: IMF has also developed tools to help governments identify and select good quality public investment projects for building low-carbon and climate-resilient infrastructure that can attract climate investments.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On RST, IMF has, indeed, requested for our contributions and MAS is assessing the request.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: RST also aims to catalyse financing from other stakeholders for climate-related projects.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, I agree with Assoc Prof Jamus Lim on the need for Singapore to play our role, including in initiatives like RST.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Here also, the multilateral development banks (MDBs), such as the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank, have crucial roles to play, as these institutions seek to crowd in private capital to close climate financing gaps, including by scaling up the use of blended finance.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And MAS will continue to work closely with IMF and the MDBs on climate financing initiatives in the region.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: On capacity-building, IMF and its training institutes, including IMF-STI, conduct training courses centred on the macro-economic implications of climate change.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These courses are targeted at policymakers from the region, including Singapore and our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I mentioned earlier, MAS has been providing funding support and guidance for STI on programmes that best meet members' capacity needs, including on the climate front.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Mr Don Wee, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim raised several questions on the different forms of financial support Singapore has provided to IMF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singapore will, indeed, continue to contribute to global efforts to bolster the IMF's resources and we will carefully assess the merits of future requests, and Parliamentary approval will be sought.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: But let me go into the different forms of financial support, even as we stand ready to assess each and every potential request.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Singapore's quota subscription of SDR 3.9 billion in IMF is a funded contribution.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is part of Singapore's Official Foreign Reserves and earns interest based on the SDR interest rate.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: A quarter of the member's quota subscription is usually paid in SDRs or foreign currencies acceptable to IMF, with the remainder paid in the member's own currency.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The portion of Singapore's quota subscription that is paid in SDRs or foreign currency can be repaid to Singapore on demand to obtain Reserve assets to meet our balance of payments financing needs, as and when that need arises.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Next, IMF also relies on borrowed resources to support its lending activity.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These currently arise, as I mentioned earlier, through the New Arrangements to Borrow (NAB) and the Bilateral Borrowing Agreements (BBAs).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Only members with strong external positions, such as Germany, Japan, Switzerland, the United States and Singapore, are requested by IMF to contribute to the NAB and BBAs.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The full list of contributors to both the NAB and BBAs respectively are available on the IMF's website.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For these loan arrangements, IMF uses standard form agreements signed across all the contributors so that the same terms apply across all contributors and there is also parity of treatment.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Third, Singapore has also contributed grants as part of the IMF's multilateral initiatives.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In November 2016, Singapore contributed a US$20 million grant to the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust (PRGT) and US$0.3 million grant to the Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust (CCRT).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: CCRT provides debt relief for the IMF's poorest and most vulnerable members in the event of a global health pandemic or natural catastrophe.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: More recently, to enhance the capacity of IMF to assist vulnerable, low-income member countries to respond to the COVID-19 pandemic, MAS provided three grants.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: To ensure transparency and accountability, MAS has issued media releases for each of these contributions on its website, in addition to publishing the information in the Government Gazette.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned, and also both Members Saktiandi Supaat and Don Wee, it is, indeed, in Singapore's interest to contribute grants to support the IMF's initiatives, such as PRGT, to assist vulnerable, low-income countries, but also provided that the BWAA safeguards are complied with.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This was explained to this House in 2016 when BWAA was last amended to empower MAS to contribute grants to IMF.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: By contributing to such initiatives, Singapore joins other members of the global community in supporting the IMF's role to safeguard global monetary and financial stability and foster sustainable growth and prosperity for its members and also to generate the goodwill that Members had mentioned.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: This will, in turn, not just generate goodwill but also benefit Singapore's economy and financial stability.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: I will now turn to Members' questions on the specific amendments proposed.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: First, let me cover questions relating to the amendment to exclude MAS' financing of IMF's operations in Singapore from the application of sections 6A(2) and 6A(3).

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The policy intent has always been, and continues to be, to apply the safeguards specific to both these sections only to grants provided to IMF to assist member countries under IMF arrangements or programmes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: These grants are different from MAS' financing of the IMF offices in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: As I mentioned in my earlier Second Reading speech, when Singapore contributes grants to support international efforts, including IMF arrangements or programmes to assist member countries in need, we do so alongside other country contributors.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, MAS cannot dictate terms because there are many other contributors to such arrangements or programmes.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: We thus have to rely on IMF to ensure there is proper governance in the administration of the grants.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Therefore, it would be prudent to subject such grants to additional domestic safeguards in sections 6A(2) and 6A(3) of BWAA, including Parliamentary oversight, which the Member had mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In contrast, the scope of MAS' financing for the IMF's offices and how it can be used are clearly stated in the respective MOUs between IMF and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS exercises direct oversight on the use of the funds, and IMF must meet MAS' reporting requirements.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Instead of Parliamentary oversight, MAS' funding of the IMF's operations in Singapore is subject to the approval of the President.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: MAS' funding of the IMF's offices in Singapore is drawn from MAS' overall budget, which requires the President's approval, pursuant to Article 22B of the Constitution read with section 166 of the MAS Act.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Presidential approval is required in every financial year, even if Past Reserves are not used.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The proposed amendment then clarifies the distinction between such funding support for IMF offices in Singapore and grants to support international efforts.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: It is also in line with the current practice for other international organisations that establish offices in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The current practice does not explicitly require Parliament to fix, by resolution, the maximum amount of grants to be given under a specific grant agreement by agencies to support the operations of Singapore-based offices of other international organisations.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: So, on the IDA question which the Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim mentioned earlier, under the IDA Act, there is no requirement, therefore, for Parliament to approve grants made by the Ministry of Finance to relevant international organisations' offices.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And the issue covered in the present amendment here, therefore, does not arise in the case of the IDA Act.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Through their regional surveillance and capacity development activities, the IMF's Singapore offices strengthen Singapore's status as a regional financial hub.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: For NAB, IMF confirmed that an arrangement can be made to facilitate repayment of a member's NAB contribution should the need arise.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: In the case of BBA, IMF confirmed that BBA cannot be suspended or prematurely terminated.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Thus, the issue of early repayment did not arise.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: The proposed amendment, therefore, provides clarity on the statutory requirements applicable to similar agreements for loans or financial assistance, based on our engagement with IMF on both the NAB as well as BBA.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Regardless, any such loans or financial assistance that are granted to IMF under BWAA will continue to be subject to strong safeguards and the risk to Singapore's Official Foreign Reserves from the absence of this early repayment option is very low.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Well, first, when Singapore provides a loan in support of IMF arrangements or programmes, Singapore, as I mentioned earlier, lends to IMF, not directly to member countries in need.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: Therefore, Singapore's loan exposure is to IMF and not to the borrowing countries.

speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
text: And finally, IMF has an excellent repayment history and has never defaulted on repayments to its creditors.
